title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
notes:
Task: Find the longest substring that can be changed into one repeated uppercase letter with at most k replacements.
Idea: Expand a sliding window and shrink it when its length minus the maximum character frequency exceeds k.
Invariant: A feasible window needs at most k replacements to make its most frequent character fill the window.
Edge cases: The recorded maximum frequency may be stale, but the standard window method still returns the correct maximum length.
complexity_reason: Each character enters and leaves the window at most once; the alphabet is fixed.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
notes:
Task: Maximize a substring length after replacing at most k characters with one repeated uppercase letter.
Idea: Maintain a frequency window and shrink while the window has more than k characters outside its most common letter.
Invariant: best stores the longest feasible window length found so far.
Edge cases: maxFreq need not be reduced when the left edge moves; this optimization still yields the correct maximum length.
complexity_reason: Both pointers move forward at most n steps and the frequency array has fixed size.

title: Construct Quad Tree
notes:
Task: Represent a square binary grid as a quadtree, using leaves for uniform regions.
Idea: Check whether the current square is uniform; if not, recursively construct its four quadrants.
Invariant: A leaf represents a region whose cells all equal its boolean value; an internal node combines four quadrant trees.
Edge cases: A 1x1 region is always uniform; Node is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Each recursive level scans its regions, and the worst-case number of internal and leaf nodes is O(n^2).

title: Construct Quad Tree
notes:
Task: Build a quadtree for a square binary grid.
Idea: Scan a region for uniformity; return a leaf if uniform, otherwise split it into four equal quadrants.
Invariant: Every returned node correctly represents exactly the square region assigned to its recursive call.
Edge cases: A uniform single-cell region becomes a leaf; Node is provided by the judge.
complexity_reason: Region scans across recursive levels process O(n^2 log n) cells in the worst case.

title: N-ary Tree Level Order Traversal
notes:
Task: Return N-ary tree values grouped by depth.
Idea: Use a queue and process the number of nodes present at the start of each level.
Invariant: At the start of each outer iteration, the queue contains exactly the nodes of the next level.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty list; Node children are traversed in their stored order.
complexity_reason: Each node is enqueued and dequeued once.

title: N-ary Tree Level Order Traversal
notes:
Task: Return each N-ary tree level as a separate list of values.
Idea: Process the queue in batches using its size at the beginning of each level.
Invariant: Children enqueued during a level are processed only in the following level.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty list; Node is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Every node is visited once and the queue can hold O(n) nodes.

title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
notes:
Task: Flatten child lists into a single doubly linked list in depth-first order.
Idea: When a node has a child, save its next node on a stack, splice in the child list, and resume saved nodes after the child chain ends.
Invariant: The processed prefix is flattened and every adjacent pair has consistent next/prev pointers.
Edge cases: Child pointers are cleared after splicing; Node is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited once and saved next pointers may be held on the stack.

title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
notes:
Task: Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list into one depth-first sequence.
Idea: Save each original next node when descending into a child list and reconnect it after the child chain ends.
Invariant: The flattened prefix maintains matching next and prev links, and no processed node retains a child pointer.
Edge cases: Null head returns null; Node is provided by the judge.
complexity_reason: Each node is processed once and the stack stores deferred next nodes.

title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
notes:
Task: Find the fewest one-character mutations from startGene to endGene using only genes in the bank.
Idea: BFS through valid genes, generating all one-position substitutions over A, C, G, and T.
Invariant: Each BFS level represents mutations at one greater distance from the start gene.
Edge cases: If start equals end return zero; if end is absent from the bank, return -1.
complexity_reason: Each bank gene is visited at most once and each position tries four possible bases.

title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
notes:
Task: Find the shortest mutation sequence using genes in the bank.
Idea: BFS over genes, generating neighbors by changing one character to each of the four DNA bases.
Invariant: The first time endGene is reached gives the minimum number of mutations.
Edge cases: A missing target gene returns -1; equal start and target returns zero.
complexity_reason: Each visited gene generates four candidates per position and is queued once.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
notes:
Task: Remove the fewest intervals so that no remaining intervals overlap.
Idea: Sort by end time and greedily keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end.
Invariant: The kept interval set has the earliest possible finishing endpoint among compatible choices.
Edge cases: Touching endpoints are non-overlapping when next.start >= last_end.
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates the greedy scan.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
notes:
Task: Find the minimum number of intervals to remove to eliminate all overlaps.
Idea: Sort by finishing time and retain each interval whose start is not before the last retained end.
Invariant: Choosing the earliest finish leaves as much room as possible for later intervals.
Edge cases: Equal boundaries do not overlap under the condition start >= end.
complexity_reason: The interval sort dominates the linear greedy scan.

title: Path Sum III
notes:
Task: Count downward paths whose node values sum to targetSum.
Idea: Maintain prefix-sum frequencies along the current root-to-node path; a prefix equal to currentSum-targetSum identifies a valid path ending here.
Invariant: prefix[p] counts ancestor-prefix sums on the current DFS path, not across unrelated branches.
Edge cases: Initialize prefix[0]=1 to count paths starting at the root; remove the current prefix count when backtracking.
complexity_reason: Each node is processed once with prefix-sum frequencies for the active path.

title: Path Sum III
notes:
Task: Count all downward paths that add up to targetSum.
Idea: Track cumulative sums on the current root-to-node path and count prior prefixes equal to currentSum-targetSum.
Invariant: The prefix map contains only prefixes from the active recursion path; counts are undone when returning from a subtree.
Edge cases: Seed prefix sum zero with count one so paths starting at the root are counted.
complexity_reason: Each node performs expected constant-time prefix-map operations and one recursive visit.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
notes:
Task: Return every start index where a length-|p| substring of s is an anagram of p.
Idea: Maintain a character-count array for a fixed-size sliding window and compare it with p's counts.
Invariant: After the window reaches length len(p), its count array represents exactly the current substring.
Edge cases: If p is longer than s, no window can match; lowercase English letters allow a fixed 26-slot array.
complexity_reason: The fixed-size alphabet arrays are compared once per window.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
notes:
Task: Find all indices where p's character multiset matches a substring of s.
Idea: Slide a window of length p and maintain two fixed-size frequency arrays.
Invariant: The window frequency array describes exactly the current length-|p| substring.
Edge cases: Return an empty list when p is longer than s; the input alphabet is lowercase English letters.
complexity_reason: The 26-entry arrays are compared at each window position.

title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
notes:
Task: Find the kth integer in lexicographical order from 1 through n.
Idea: Count how many values lie beneath the current decimal prefix and skip whole prefix subtrees when k is larger than that count.
Invariant: curr is the current lexical prefix; k is the one-based rank remaining within the unvisited lexical sequence.
Edge cases: The prefix count uses an exclusive upper bound n+1 and expands prefix ranges by powers of ten.
complexity_reason: Each lexical move counts prefix levels, and there are O(log n) digits and O(log n) moves in the traversal bound.

title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
notes:
Task: Return the kth number in dictionary order among integers 1 through n.
Idea: Count the size of each prefix's subtree and either skip it or descend to its first child.
Invariant: curr identifies the current prefix and k is the rank offset after the current value.
Edge cases: Long arithmetic is used for prefix boundaries to avoid overflow while multiplying by ten.
complexity_reason: Each subtree count scans digit-length levels and the traversal performs a logarithmic number of prefix moves.

title: Arranging Coins
notes:
Task: Find the largest number of complete staircase rows that can be formed from n coins.
Idea: Binary-search k using the triangular-number condition k(k+1)/2 <= n.
Invariant: The search interval brackets the greatest feasible complete-row count.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; integer arithmetic avoids floating-point square-root rounding.
complexity_reason: The binary-search interval halves each iteration.

title: Arranging Coins
notes:
Task: Return the number of complete rows in a coin staircase.
Idea: Binary-search the greatest k whose triangular number does not exceed n.
Invariant: Values at or below the feasible boundary can form complete rows; values above it require too many coins.
Edge cases: Use long multiplication for k(k+1) to avoid overflow.
complexity_reason: The candidate interval is halved until the maximum feasible row count remains.
